title: Short Stuff: Pollen Count
summary: Short Stuff episode on how pollen counts are actually made. Chuck has been suffering from allergies, and the hosts explain that pollen is the plant's male gametophyte from anthers, that individual grains are microscopic but clump into visible drifts, and that wind-borne pollen is what matters for allergies. A pollen count is the number of grains per cubic meter of air over 24 hours, measured with volumetric air samplers: the rotating arm impactor (Rotorod, greased rods spinning around 2,400 rpm) and the Hirst-type spore trap (Burkard sampler, greased microscope slide moving 2 mm per hour). Palynologists count the grains under a microscope; sampling frequency and operators vary by city, and certification comes through the National Allergy Bureau or the American Academy of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology. The episode closes with other uses of pollen: fossil palynology for dating strata and reconstructing ancient climates and plants, and forensic palynology in crime investigations.

segments.title: Opening banter and Chuck's allergies
segments.summary: Hosts open the Short Stuff episode; Chuck describes two months of allergies and mentions the earlier full pollen episode. They introduce the question of how pollen counts are obtained.

segments.title: What pollen is and why it piles up
segments.summary: Pollen is the plant's male gametophyte from the anthers that fertilizes the carpel. Individual grains are 10 to 100 micrometers and clump into visible drifts, such as those in Georgia in spring, and bake onto cars and decks.

segments.title: Wind-borne pollen and allergies
segments.summary: Insect-pollinated pollen is less of an issue; wind-borne pollen from less showy plants such as grasses, trees, and weeds is what gets airborne, enters the mucous membranes, and is what pollen counts measure.

segments.title: Pollen identification teaser
segments.summary: Chuck notes that news reports sometimes name specific pollen types such as ragweed, which requires knowing what each type's grain looks like. Josh previews how counting is done after a break.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the explanation of pollen counting.

segments.title: Defining the pollen count and certified counters
segments.summary: A pollen count is the number of grains per cubic meter of air over a 24-hour period. Chuck references a meteorologist, Katie Walls, certified through an Atlanta allergy group, and notes certification from the National Allergy Bureau or the American Academy of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology.
topics: American Academy of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology

segments.title: Volumetric air samplers: rotating arm and Hirst-type
segments.summary: Two volumetric samplers are described. The rotating arm impactor (Rotorod) spins at about 2,400 rpm with greased rods that catch pollen. The Hirst-type spore trap (Burkard sampler) draws in air over 24 hours onto a greased microscope slide.

segments.title: Hour-by-hour slide and palynologists counting
segments.summary: The Hirst-type slide moves inward at 2 mm per hour, so hourly pollen levels can be read. Palynologists examine samples under a microscope and count the grains.

segments.title: Variation in sampling practices
segments.summary: Sampling frequency varies: daily for a year, weekdays only, or a few days a week. Operators can be county health departments or allergists contracted by news stations. Cost is a factor for cities.

segments.title: Putting pollen numbers in perspective
segments.summary: A cubic meter is about three feet on each side. Hosts say a count of 3,000 grains is very high and sounds dramatic when visualized as air inhaled over 24 hours.

segments.title: Where pollen counters should be placed
segments.summary: Hosts speculate about where to place counters, such as near forest edges versus parking lots. They note that placement near a forest could skew counts and make counting harder.

segments.title: Forensic and fossil palynology
segments.summary: Besides allergies, pollen is used in forensic palynology to link people to crime scenes and in fossil palynology to learn about ancient plants and climate. Pollen morphology stays stable over millions of years, so fossil ragweed pollen would show that ragweed grew in a given stratum.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the short episode with Chuck saying he has a runny nose and Josh wishing him luck. The episode closes with the standard iHeartRadio production credit.
